sourceNotes: Seeded from HLM roleplay performance indicators and hospitality and tourism cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: HLM event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the hospitality and tourism cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: A hotel's revenue per available room divided by the competitive set's, times 100 — 100 means the property is capturing exactly its fair share, 112 means it is taking 12% more revenue per room than its share of the market's rooms would predict.
terms.whyItMatters: STR-report roleplays hand you a property at 92 and ask what to do; the index tells you the hotel is losing share even in a year its own RevPAR rose, which a raw dollar figure hides.

terms.definition: Occupancy divided by the competitive set's occupancy, times 100 — it isolates how well a hotel fills rooms independently of what it charges for them, so a property can score 118 here while losing money on rate.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge asks why a full hotel is underperforming, the answer is an MPI above 100 paired with an ARI below 100: it is buying occupancy with discounts.

terms.definition: A property's average daily rate divided by the competitive set's, times 100; multiplied by the occupancy index and divided by 100 it reproduces the RevPAR index exactly, which is why the three are read as one triangle.
terms.whyItMatters: Given MPI 105 and ARI 90, a competitor must be able to say RevPAR index is 94.5 and recommend rate discipline rather than more discounting.

terms.definition: The percentage of a competitive set's total room supply a hotel owns — 150 rooms in a 1,000-room comp set is 15%, and that 15% is the baseline any occupancy or revenue index is measured against.
terms.whyItMatters: Adding a 200-room competitor drops the same hotel's fair share to 12.5%; a rooms-division case turns on recognizing that the index moved because supply moved, not because the hotel got worse.

terms.definition: Gross operating profit divided by available room nights — unlike a top-line rooms metric it nets out every department's revenue and every controllable expense, so it moves with flow-through and can fall in a quarter when RevPAR rises.
terms.whyItMatters: Owner and asset-manager roleplays are graded on profit per room, not revenue per room; a discount program that lifts RevPAR while adding labor and commission cost shows up here as a loss.

terms.definition: Actual rooms revenue divided by potential rooms revenue — the dollars a hotel would earn selling every room at rack — expressed as a percentage, so 100% occupancy at half price scores 50%.
terms.whyItMatters: A revenue-management roleplay that praises a sold-out night is testing whether you can compute the yield and show the sellout was bought with rate the property did not need to give away.

terms.definition: A bottom-up room-pricing method that starts from the owner's required return on investment, adds income tax, fixed charges, operating expenses and other departments' losses, then divides the total by forecast rooms sold to yield the rate the property must average.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to justify a rate to an owner rather than to the market, a competitor works this backwards from the desired profit; a bottom-line target of $1.2M over 40,000 room nights sets a floor no competitive shop can override.

terms.definition: Guests in house minus rooms sold, divided by rooms sold — 320 guests in 250 occupied rooms is 28%, and that figure, not the room count, forecasts breakfast covers, amenity par and housekeeping linen draw.
terms.whyItMatters: A group booked at two guests per room changes the F&B and labor forecast even though the rooms number is unchanged; hospitality cases hide the labor overrun in exactly that gap.

terms.definition: The arithmetic that compares the revenue a low-rate group would bring against the higher-rate transient business it would push out on the same dates, counting the ancillary spend of each, before a group rate is quoted.
terms.whyItMatters: A group asking for 80 rooms at $119 on a night forecast to sell out at $189 is a net loss of roughly $5,600 in rooms revenue; the roleplay wants that number computed before the discount is refused.

terms.definition: The full price of relocating an oversold guest — a comparable room paid at the receiving hotel, transportation, a phone call home, plus the recovery gesture and the lost future value of the relationship — which is what the overbooking level must stay cheaper than.
terms.whyItMatters: Overbooking questions are decided by comparing this figure against the average rate lost to a no-show; if walking costs $340 and an empty room costs $150, the property overbooks less aggressively.

terms.definition: The historical percentage of guaranteed reservations that never arrive, segmented by market and day of week, applied to the reservations on the books to set how many rooms above capacity may safely be sold.
terms.whyItMatters: With 400 rooms, 400 on the books and a 6% factor for corporate midweek, a competitor sells 24 more rooms rather than guessing; the roleplay is graded on showing the multiplication.

terms.definition: Total rooms less out-of-order rooms, less stayovers, less reservations, plus expected understays and no-shows — the arithmetic that says how many rooms may still be sold for tonight, which is never simply capacity minus reservations.
terms.whyItMatters: A front-office roleplay hands you the house count and asks whether a walk-in can be accommodated; forgetting the understay and no-show additions leaves rooms empty that were sellable.

terms.definition: A distribution-contract obligation to publish no lower price on any other channel than the one given to the contracting intermediary, which is why a hotel undercuts online travel agencies with member-only closed rates and added value rather than a lower public price.
terms.whyItMatters: When an owner demands the website beat the OTA, a competitor must explain the clause and route the answer through a loyalty log-in rate — several European jurisdictions have narrowed or banned the wide form, and quoting that distinction earns the point.

terms.definition: Average daily rate less all distribution cost — commission, transaction fee, loyalty charge — divided by the average daily rate; a $200 booking carrying $36 of channel cost yields 82%, so it is worth less than a $180 direct booking.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-mix roleplays are won by ranking sources on this rather than on rate, because the highest-rate channel is routinely the least profitable one.

terms.definition: A negotiated-account clause requiring the hotel to honor the contracted rate for as long as any room of that type remains unsold, stripping away the length-of-stay and closed-date fences revenue management would otherwise apply.
terms.whyItMatters: A corporate account demanding it on a citywide sellout date is asking the hotel to give up its highest-rate night; the roleplay wants the displacement cost quantified before the clause is conceded.

terms.definition: The multiple of a full house a property stocks of a circulating item — three par of linen means one set on the bed, one in the laundry cycle and one on the shelf, so a 200-room hotel buys 600 sets, not 200.
terms.whyItMatters: Housekeeping budget roleplays turn on this multiplication; ordering one par is the error that strands a property when the laundry goes down and forces emergency purchasing at retail.

terms.definition: The workload unit behind a housekeeping schedule — a standard guestroom counts as one and takes about half an hour, a suite or a checkout counts as more, and a full eight-hour shift carries roughly fifteen of them after breaks and briefing.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to staff 240 occupied rooms, a competitor divides by the credit standard to get sixteen attendants and can defend the number to a general manager who wants twelve.

terms.definition: A department's controllable expense divided by rooms actually sold rather than rooms available, which makes it the only labor or supply figure that can be compared honestly between a 45% and an 85% occupancy month.
terms.whyItMatters: A housekeeping manager whose total payroll rose in a strong month is defended by showing this measure fell; the exam item is testing the occupied-versus-available denominator.

terms.definition: The set of nonguest receivable accounts — direct-bill companies, travel-agency commissions, bad checks, late charges — that a folio is transferred into once the guest has departed, moving the balance out of the in-house ledger and into collections aging.
terms.whyItMatters: Night-audit questions ask where a departed guest's unpaid balance lives; putting it in the guest ledger overstates in-house accounts and hides an aging receivable the controller must chase.

terms.definition: The maximum balance a property will let a folio reach before intervention, set by management and usually well above the card issuer's own floor limit; crossing it puts the account on the high-balance report the night audit generates.
terms.whyItMatters: A long-stay guest whose incidentals pass the threshold has to be re-authorized before the stay continues, and the roleplay is graded on handling that conversation without accusing the guest.

terms.definition: A percentage of gross revenue, commonly around 4% and escrowed monthly under the management or franchise agreement, that may only be spent on replacing soft goods and case goods — never on operating shortfalls or debt service.
terms.whyItMatters: When a brand mandates a renovation, whether the owner can fund it comes down to the balance this clause has built; an owner who negotiated 2% to protect cash flow is the standard case-study conflict.

terms.definition: The operator's second fee, computed as a share of gross operating profit earned only above an owner's stated priority return, and stacked on a base fee taken off total revenue whether or not the hotel makes money.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why an operator paid 3% of revenue plus 10% of profit over the owner's priority pushes GOPPAR rather than occupancy, and a management-agreement roleplay wants that incentive alignment named.

terms.definition: The lowest unrestricted, publicly bookable price for a given date and room type — no advance purchase, no minimum stay, fully cancellable — which is the ceiling every discount and the reference every parity clause is measured from.
terms.whyItMatters: Guests who ask why last night cost less are answered by explaining this is a date-by-date figure, not a fixed price list, and every negotiated discount is quoted as a percentage off it.

terms.definition: The lift in direct bookings a hotel gets purely from being visible on an online travel agency, where the shopper finds the property on the intermediary and then books on the brand site instead.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the argument against pulling out of an OTA to save commission — the listing was also the advertising, and the direct bookings it fed disappear with it.

terms.definition: The daily close of the hotel's accounting day — posting room and tax charges, reconciling every department's outlets to the property management system, verifying no-shows and rolling the business date forward.
terms.whyItMatters: Front-office roleplays about a disputed charge or an unbalanced shift depend on knowing when the day closes and what a late charge does once it has.

terms.definition: The brand-mandated schedule of renovations and equipment upgrades an owner must complete, on a stated deadline, as a condition of a new franchise license, a change of ownership or a license renewal.
terms.whyItMatters: A conversion roleplay hangs on telling an owner that the flag comes with a multimillion-dollar capital obligation, not just a royalty rate.

terms.definition: A capital contribution a brand or operator advances to an owner to win a management or franchise deal, amortized across the agreement's term and repayable on a pro-rata basis if the owner terminates early.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the concession an owner asks for when two brands are competing for the same site, and the clawback is what keeps the owner from flipping flags two years later.

terms.definition: A candidate group qualifies as a market segment only if it passes five named tests — measurable (its size and buying power can be quantified), substantial (large and profitable enough to serve alone), accessible (reachable through some channel or medium), differentiable (it responds differently from other segments to a change in the mix) and actionable (the firm can actually build and run a program for it); failing any one of the five makes it a description of people, not a segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Market-planning roleplays that ask you to defend a chosen segment are scored on running it against the criteria out loud; the segment competitors usually pick fails 'substantial' or 'accessible'.

terms.definition: Helping customers make purchase decisions through planned communication.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling vocabulary supports recommendations about staff, service, and revenue.

terms.definition: Adjusting communication and approach to cultural and social differences.
terms.whyItMatters: Culturally aware service builds stronger, more diverse relationships.

terms.definition: Price of one currency in another, derived from each one's quote against a third: if $1 buys €0.90 and $1 buys £0.80, then €1 buys £0.889, since 0.80 ÷ 0.90 = 0.889. Any quoted pair that disagrees with that division is an arbitrage opportunity, which is why the three quotes stay consistent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exchange-rate items quote two currencies against the dollar and ask what a euro invoice costs a British subsidiary — a division, not a lookup.

terms.definition: A company-wide philosophy making every employee responsible for continuous improvement and customer-defined quality; quality assurance is the narrower set of process activities designed to prevent defects, and quality control is the narrowest — the inspection and testing that finds defects after production.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items line up the three terms and ask which one an inspection station belongs to; sorting philosophy from prevention from detection is the whole question.

terms.definition: Occurs when a party makes clear before performance is due that it will not perform, letting the other side treat the contract as breached at once, suspend its own performance, and sue without waiting for the due date. UCC section 2-609 adds a softer middle step: a party with reasonable grounds for insecurity may demand written assurance and suspend performance until it arrives, treating silence past thirty days as a repudiation.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a supplier emails that it probably cannot ship the spring order tests whether that is a repudiation or only grounds to demand assurance.

terms.definition: Planning, developing, marketing, and managing offerings across their life.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures offerings meet customer needs and generate sustainable revenue.

terms.definition: Promise of company shares delivered on a vesting date and taxed as ordinary income on the full market value at vest — 400 shares vesting at $50 is $20,000 of W-2 wages whether or not a single share is sold. A stock option instead taxes the spread at exercise and is worth nothing while the price sits below the strike, which this grant never is.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two offers in a roleplay is impossible without valuing the equity: the exam wants shares times price times the vesting fraction, plus the tax hit at vest.

terms.definition: Communication that informs, persuades, and reminds customers about offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion choices must fit the audience, message, and budget.

terms.definition: The amount or percentage added to a product's cost to set its selling price.
terms.whyItMatters: Markup links cost directly to a pricing recommendation.

terms.definition: Profit from selling an asset for more than its purchase price, taxable only once the sale happens and taxed at a lower rate when the asset was held over a year.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment scenarios ask whether a client owes tax on a stock that has risen in value; unrealized gains are not taxed until sold.

terms.definition: The medium — email, phone, in person, memo — chosen for a message.
terms.whyItMatters: Justifying channel choice signals professional maturity.

terms.definition: The blend of product, price, place, and promotion used to reach a target market.
terms.whyItMatters: The four Ps are the standard framework for building a marketing recommendation.

terms.definition: Deals won divided by every qualified opportunity worked in the period — 15 wins out of 60 qualified opportunities is 25%. The denominator keeps opportunities that are still open or that ended in no decision, which is exactly what win rate throws out, so this figure always reads lower than win rate for the same rep.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sales-management roleplay that asks you to diagnose a rep whose revenue is falling, a dropping close rate against a steady win rate points at unqualified prospecting rather than weak closing technique.

terms.definition: A queuing formula that converts contact volume, average handle time and a target answer speed into required agents, and its output is non-linear: doubling volume needs well under double the staff, while removing the last agent from a tight schedule can multiply wait time. Averages alone cannot produce the answer because arrivals are random, not evenly spaced.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains the counter-intuitive result in a staffing case — cutting one agent from a 20-agent schedule can break an 80/20 target outright.

terms.definition: Export price index divided by import price index, times 100. A country whose export prices climb 6% while import prices climb 2% moves from 100 to about 104 and can buy more foreign goods per unit shipped; a commodity exporter watching prices slide sees the figure drop even with export volume flat.
terms.whyItMatters: Trade-alliance and global-environment questions ask who gained from a shift in world prices, and the ratio of the two indexes settles it.

terms.definition: An energy-control procedure requiring every power source to a machine to be isolated, physically locked, and tagged by the individual servicing it — with the rule that only that person may remove their own lock — so no one can restart equipment while a colleague is inside it.
terms.whyItMatters: Equipment-safety roleplays about a maintenance injury expect this named procedure and the one-worker-one-lock rule, not general advice to turn the machine off.

terms.definition: Creating agreement and buy-in across a group with differing viewpoints.
terms.whyItMatters: It secures team alignment and commitment to shared decisions.

terms.definition: Counts how many separate product lines a company carries, never how many items sit inside them: a grocer running dairy, bakery, and frozen lines has a width of 3 even when those lines hold 400 items between them, while product mix depth counts the items within one line.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix-planning roleplay that asks how a retailer should expand expects width and depth reported as two different counts; answering with adjectives like 'broad' instead of a number loses the indicator.

terms.definition: Subtraction run one competency at a time — required proficiency minus current proficiency — with the resulting gaps ranked by size multiplied by how critical the competency is, so a 2-point gap on a critical skill outranks a 3-point gap on a peripheral one. Without the criticality weighting it degenerates into a list of everything someone cannot do.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on assessing your own interests and skills against an employer's expectations is really asking for this weighted subtraction.

terms.definition: Reach multiplied by average frequency, the one number that sizes a schedule's total weight: 40% of the target seen four times is 160. The same 160 can be bought as 80% reach at 2.0 frequency, which is why the figure alone never describes a schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-planning items hand the competitor a reach figure and a frequency figure and ask for the schedule's weight, or give the weight and one factor and ask for the other; a roleplay defending a media plan to a client is expected to state both halves, not just the total.

terms.definition: A measure of how much customer demand responds to a price change.
terms.whyItMatters: Elasticity predicts demand shifts and helps optimize price for revenue.

terms.definition: How easily an asset can be converted to cash without losing much value.
terms.whyItMatters: Liquidity explains why a profitable business can still run short of cash.

terms.definition: Employees present at both the start and the end of a period, divided by the headcount at the start, times 100 — 190 of 200 starters still present is 95%. It is not simply 100 minus the turnover rate, because turnover uses average headcount and counts departures of people hired mid-period, while retention ignores anyone hired after the start date.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you a turnover figure and ask for retention; subtracting from 100 is the trap, and the different denominators are the tested point.

terms.definition: Empirical pattern in which roughly the top 20% of a category's buyers generate about 80% of its volume, and the heavier half of buyers accounts for 80% to 90% of units in many packaged-goods categories — so a 10% lift among heavy users is worth several times the same percentage lift among light users, and a promotion measured in customers reached can be worth less than one measured in volume reached.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion-budget roleplays that ask where to spend a limited fund are won by weighting the target by consumption share rather than by headcount.

terms.definition: The structured steps that move a customer from awareness to purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the process helps competitors execute each stage well.

terms.definition: Fully loaded center cost — wages, benefits, technology and facilities — divided by contacts handled; $180,000 a month across 30,000 contacts is $6.00 each. A live phone contact typically runs several times the cost of a self-service session, and that spread, not the software licence, is the business case for deflection.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a chatbot or a help center has to set this figure against the deflected channel to justify the spend.

terms.definition: A fixed list of goods and quantities repriced each period; this period's cost divided by the base period's cost, times 100, is the index. A $2,400 basket against a $2,000 base year prints 120, meaning prices are 20% above base — and because the quantities never change, substitution toward cheaper goods is invisible and the index overstates the true rise.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation-impact questions ask a competitor to compute an index from two years of basket costs and then explain why the printed rate overstates what shoppers actually pay.

terms.definition: Outsourcing physical distribution functions — warehousing, transportation, freight handling — to a provider that owns trucks and buildings; a fourth-party provider owns no assets and instead manages the other providers, acting as a single coordinating layer over several third parties.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution-strategy questions ask which outsourcing level fits a firm that lacks not trucks but the ability to coordinate several carriers, and the asset-owning versus orchestrating split is the answer.

terms.definition: An organized, computer-managed collection of related data that can be stored and retrieved systematically.
terms.whyItMatters: Businesses run everything from inventory to customer records on databases.

terms.definition: The stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline.
terms.whyItMatters: The stage a product is in drives its marketing, pricing, and distribution.

terms.definition: Pay increase tied to a published price index rather than to performance — Social Security's 2.5% raise for 2025 came directly from the CPI-W. Relocation uses the same arithmetic: moving a $60,000 salary to a city with a cost index of 130 against a base of 100 takes $78,000 to hold the same purchasing power.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay weighing a transfer offer to a more expensive city is scored on running the index ratio, not on comparing the two base salaries.

terms.definition: The blend of advertising, publicity, sales promotion, and personal selling.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix lets competitors recommend more than one communication path.

terms.definition: The percentage of revenue left as profit after costs are subtracted.
terms.whyItMatters: Margin reflects pricing effectiveness against financial goals.

terms.definition: Matching a checkbook or ledger against a bank statement by adjusting both sides — outstanding checks and deposits in transit on the bank's, fees and interest on the depositor's.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance exam item gives a statement balance and a book balance and asks for the true cash figure; only adjusting one side gets it wrong.

terms.definition: A firm's obligations beyond profit, organized in Carroll's pyramid as economic, then legal, then ethical, then philanthropic layers, where the lower layers are required and the top layer is desired; the ordering is what stops it from being read as charity alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics exam items ask which layer a described action occupies, and community donations by a firm that is violating labor law is the classic mis-ordering trap.

terms.definition: One brand's sales to a single customer divided by that customer's total category spending over the same period — a household that spends $400 a year on coffee and $120 of it at one chain gives that chain 30% — so it is a per-customer ratio, unlike market share, which divides a brand's sales by the whole category's sales across all buyers; a brand can hold flat market share while its wallet share collapses.
terms.whyItMatters: Customer-relations roleplays that ask how to grow revenue without new customers are answered with this ratio and the cross-sell that raises it.

terms.definition: Deals won divided only by the deals that reached a final decision — wins plus losses — so 15 wins among 45 resolved deals is 33%, with open and no-decision opportunities excluded from the denominator entirely. That narrower denominator is the whole difference from close rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that hand you a pipeline table expect you to notice which opportunities belong in the denominator; counting still-open deals as losses is the single most common wrong answer.

terms.definition: Systems and strategies for managing customer data, interactions, and relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: CRM tracks preferences and delivers personalized service at scale.

terms.definition: The forward premium on a currency has to equal the gap between the two countries' interest rates, or borrowing in one and lending in the other earns a riskless profit. A 5% domestic rate against 2% abroad implies the foreign currency trades forward about 3% above spot, which cancels the yield advantage exactly.
terms.whyItMatters: International-finance items ask why a competitor should not simply park cash in the highest-yielding currency; the forward discount is the answer.

terms.definition: A structured visit by managers to the actual place work happens, to observe the process and ask questions rather than to inspect people or correct anyone on the spot — the no-blame, observe-only rule is what keeps workers from staging the process for the visitor.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how a manager should diagnose a slow process, the expected answer is direct observation at the work site rather than a report or a meeting, which is what an operations judge is listening for.

terms.definition: The overall approach a business uses to reach customers and meet marketing goals.
terms.whyItMatters: Case studies require strategies that fit business objectives and market conditions.

terms.definition: Counts the individual items inside a single line -- sizes, flavors, formulations, models: a toothpaste line of 4 flavors in 3 tube sizes is 12 items deep, and adding a fifth flavor deepens the mix without widening it, because width counts lines alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a table of lines and items and ask for one number; students who add every item in the company report the length instead of the depth of the line asked about.

terms.definition: Development instrument that collects ratings from four vantage points — self, manager, peers and direct reports, usually 8 to 12 raters in total — and reports where the self-rating and everyone else's diverge. A performance appraisal is single-source and administrative, feeding pay and promotion, which is exactly why these results are normally kept out of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on using development resources is scored on knowing this tool informs growth, and that folding it into a pay decision makes raters stop being honest.

terms.definition: Rating points counted only against the demographic actually being bought instead of against every household in the market, so a broad-appeal buy delivering 200 gross rating points may deliver just 60 of these if only 30% of its viewers fall inside the target.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows a schedule looking strong on total weight but thin on the buying demographic is testing this distinction, and a media-plan roleplay that quotes only the gross figure to a client buying an 18-to-34 audience has hidden the waste.

terms.definition: Expresses the dollar markup as a percentage of what the merchandise cost the seller: (retail - cost) / cost. A $40 item ticketed at $100 carries a 150% markup on cost but only a 60% markup on retail; convert between them with markup-on-retail = markup-on-cost / (1 + markup-on-cost).
terms.whyItMatters: Merchandising math items hand a competitor one percentage and ask for the other selling price, and dividing by retail when the problem said cost throws off every later step of the calculation.

terms.definition: Paying a loan off through fixed installments split between interest and principal, with the interest share largest at the start and shrinking every payment.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask why an early mortgage payment barely reduces the balance; the amortization split is the reason, not a fee.

terms.definition: A sum the parties fix in the contract as the remedy for breach, enforceable only if two things hold: actual harm was difficult to estimate when the contract was signed, and the figure is a reasonable forecast of that harm. A number set far above probable loss is an unenforceable penalty, which throws the injured party back on proving real compensatory damages item by item.
terms.whyItMatters: Construction and event-contract roleplays ask whether a $500-per-day late clause will hold up, and the two-part reasonableness test is the answer.

terms.definition: A philosophy that focuses all business activities on satisfying customer needs profitably.
terms.whyItMatters: It reminds competitors that every tactic should trace back to a real customer need.

terms.definition: Identifying and qualifying potential customers who may need an offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Effective prospecting builds the foundation for successful sales.

terms.definition: Closed cases a customer reopens divided by cases closed in the period — 60 of 1,200 is 5%. It is the audit on first contact resolution: an agent can inflate the resolution figure by closing tickets early, and this is the only metric that catches it, which is why the two are always reported as a pair.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-quality case, the competitor who pairs a resolution claim with this check shows the judge they know the headline metric can be gamed.

terms.definition: Share of each extra dollar of income that leaves the country for foreign goods. It enters the multiplier as a leakage, turning 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) into 1 ÷ (1 − MPC + MPI): with MPC 0.8 the closed figure of 5 falls to 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.1) = 3.33 once a tenth of new income is spent abroad.
terms.whyItMatters: Globalization questions ask why a stimulus works less well in a highly open economy; the leakage in the denominator is the mechanism.

terms.definition: A solicitation that describes a problem and invites vendors to propose their own solution, approach and price, evaluated on weighted criteria beyond cost — where a request for quotation specifies the exact item and quantity already and asks only for price and delivery, making it a lowest-bidder instrument.
terms.whyItMatters: Bid-process roleplays turn on choosing the right document: asking for solutions when you already know the specification wastes vendor effort, and asking only for price on an undefined need produces incomparable bids.

terms.definition: Scores a passage from 0 to 100 where a HIGHER number means easier, running opposite in direction to every grade-level formula: 206.835 - 1.015 x (words per sentence) - 84.6 x (syllables per word). The 60-to-70 band is the plain-English range consumer documents target, 30 and below is college-graduate difficulty, and 90-100 is fifth-grade text. Because the scale runs to 100, a score of 70 is good here while a grade-level score of 70 would be absurd.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items and written-event judges both hand you a score and ask whether the document suits its audience; reading this 0-to-100 scale as though it were a grade level reverses your answer.

terms.definition: A group of related products sold under one brand or category.
terms.whyItMatters: Line decisions balance customer choice against cost and complexity.

terms.definition: Earnings measured in what they buy rather than in dollars received: a 3% raise against 4% inflation is a cut of roughly 1%, since 1.03 divided by 1.04 comes to 0.99. The nominal number on the offer letter can rise every single year while this one falls, which is why a raise is judged against the inflation rate and not against last year's salary.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item giving a raise percentage and an inflation rate is asking for this comparison, and the trap answer is the one that calls any raise an improvement.

terms.definition: Paid, nonpersonal communication delivered through media to large audiences.
terms.whyItMatters: Advertising builds broad brand awareness efficiently and at scale.

terms.definition: A plan for setting prices to meet business objectives and positioning.
terms.whyItMatters: A sound strategy is central to case presentations and positioning.

terms.definition: Current assets divided by current liabilities, the standard test of whether a business can cover what it owes within the next twelve months.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance exam items hand over a balance sheet and ask whether the firm can meet short-term obligations; a ratio under 1.0 is the answer that says no.

terms.definition: Bandura's task-specific confidence that you can carry out a particular action, built from four sources in descending order of power — a personal mastery experience, watching a similar person succeed, verbal persuasion, and how one reads one's own physical arousal. Self-esteem, by contrast, is a global judgment of personal worth, so a person can hold high esteem and low efficacy on one specific task.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking how a manager raises a nervous employee's confidence for a first presentation wants a staged small success rather than a pep talk, since mastery outranks persuasion.

terms.definition: The percentage of a category's national sales occurring in one market divided by the percentage of the national population living there, multiplied by 100 — a metro holding 2% of the population but 3% of category sales scores 150 — where 100 is exactly average and anything above it means the category is over-developed in that market regardless of how any single brand performs there.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-allocation roleplays ask which markets deserve the spend; the index pair, not gut feel about city size, is what a judge expects to hear.

terms.definition: Open opportunity value divided by the quota for the period: $900,000 of open deals against a $300,000 quota is 3x, the usual rule of thumb for a team that wins about one deal in three. Coverage below the reciprocal of the win rate means the quota is arithmetically unreachable no matter how well the rep sells.
terms.whyItMatters: A district-manager roleplay judged on forecasting expects you to test coverage before promising a number, and to prescribe prospecting rather than closing coaching when coverage is thin.

terms.definition: The clock from a customer's message to the first substantive human reply, which stops on that reply even though nothing is fixed yet; resolution time runs on until the issue is actually closed. A 1-hour response with a 3-day resolution is a legitimate and common pair, and quoting one figure for both makes a team look twice as fast as it is.
terms.whyItMatters: Email and social-service roleplays set two separate targets, so a competitor who reports a single number has misread the case.

terms.definition: Splits output growth into three addends — the contribution of added capital, the contribution of added hours, and the residual left over. If output rises 4% while capital and labor together explain 2.5%, the remaining 1.5% is productivity growth, the only piece that raises income per worker permanently.
terms.whyItMatters: Productivity items ask a competitor to separate growth that came from hiring more people from growth that came from each worker producing more.

terms.definition: Assigning each item a storage location based on picking velocity, unit weight and case cube, so the fastest-moving lines sit closest to packing at waist height — the objective is minimizing picker travel distance, which is the largest single component of order-fulfillment labor.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution roleplays about slow order fulfillment expect a layout answer tied to pick frequency, not more staff, and the travel-time argument is what makes it persuasive.

terms.definition: The process of orienting and integrating new employees into the organization.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong onboarding speeds productivity and conveys company values and procedures.

terms.definition: Total number of items across every line the firm sells, equal to width multiplied by average depth: 5 lines averaging 8 items each gives a length of 40, so a company can lengthen its mix without widening it by adding items to lines it already runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Product-mix questions hand you width and average depth and expect the multiplication; a roleplay judge scoring a merchandising plan looks for the total item count you commit the buyer to carrying.

terms.definition: Written 30-, 60- or 90-day document listing measurable targets, the support the employer will provide and the stated consequence of missing them. It is not progressive discipline's verbal-then-written-warning ladder: discipline addresses conduct the employee chose, this addresses capability, and it doubles as the documentation trail for a for-cause termination.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervision roleplay about an employee who is trying hard and still missing quota calls for this, while a no-call-no-show calls for the discipline ladder instead.

terms.definition: One percent of all the households or people in a market's universe, counted whether or not their set is switched on, so a program watched by 90,000 homes in a 1,500,000-household market rates 6.0.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost-per-point math on the marketing exam starts here, and competitors lose the item by treating the figure as a share of viewers rather than a percent of the whole market.

terms.definition: Divides the same dollar markup by the selling price instead of by the cost: (retail - cost) / retail. It is the form buyers and merchandise plans quote, it always reads lower than the cost-based figure on the same item, and it converts back with markup-on-cost = markup-on-retail / (1 - markup-on-retail).
terms.whyItMatters: In a retail-buying roleplay a judge states margins the way the trade states them, so a candidate has to convert a vendor's quoted markup before comparing it to the store's own target.

terms.definition: Current assets minus inventory, divided by current liabilities — the stricter liquidity test, because inventory may not convert to cash in time to pay a bill.
terms.whyItMatters: A retailer with a healthy current ratio and a weak quick ratio is the classic exam case, and the difference is inventory the business cannot sell fast.

terms.definition: The four guarantees a relational transaction makes — atomicity, meaning all steps commit or none do; consistency, meaning no declared rule is left broken; isolation, meaning concurrent transactions cannot read each other's partial work; and durability, meaning a committed write survives a crash — and precisely the set that BASE-style distributed stores relax in exchange for availability.
terms.whyItMatters: A banking-transfer scenario asks what keeps a debit from posting when the matching credit fails, and the graded answer names atomicity within this set rather than saying the system is careful.

terms.definition: The bundle of benefits a business promises to deliver to a specific customer group.
terms.whyItMatters: A sharp value proposition anchors positioning, messaging, and pricing.

terms.definition: The opening contact and strategy used to engage a potential customer.
terms.whyItMatters: A professional approach sets the first impression that drives interest.

terms.definition: Contacts passed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier divided by total contacts. A transfer moves a contact sideways to a peer queue; an escalation moves it up a level of authority — so an agent whose refund limit is $50 must escalate every $60 refund, and the rate is measuring the policy, not the customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about empowering frontline staff turn on this: raising an agent's approval limit is usually the cheapest way to cut it.

terms.definition: Fraction of checkable deposits a bank is barred from lending — mandated reserves ÷ deposits. At 10%, a $1,000 deposit locks up $100 and frees $900, and the ceiling on deposit creation is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; cutting the ratio to 5% doubles that ceiling without the central bank buying a single security.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate-fluctuation items ask how a change in this one fraction moves the amount of money in circulation, and the answer is the reciprocal.

terms.definition: An INTERNAL request from a department asking purchasing to buy something, carrying no commitment to any outside party; the purchase order that purchasing then issues is the EXTERNAL document, and it is the offer that forms a binding contract when the supplier accepts it.
terms.whyItMatters: Purchasing-control questions ask which document a department head signs and which one legally obligates the company; treating the internal request as the order is the standard error.

terms.definition: Relocating a business activity to another country while the firm still owns and runs it; outsourcing instead transfers the activity to an outside company that may sit in the same city, so the two axes are ownership and geography and a move can be one, the other, or both.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a firm opening its own support center abroad and expect the correct label, with 'outsourcing' as the planted distractor.

terms.definition: Building a company's overall reputation and identity across its offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong corporate branding creates loyalty and justifies premium pricing.

terms.definition: Seven-factor analysis the Department of Labor applies to decide whether an unpaid intern is really an employee: who gains the greater benefit, whether the work is tied to academic credit, whether it displaces paid staff, and whether either side expects a paid job at the end. If the employer is the main beneficiary, minimum wage and overtime are owed retroactively.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship roleplay staffing a startup with unpaid interns is scored on this test, because failing it turns free labor into back wages.

terms.definition: Short-term incentives like coupons, contests, and discounts that spur purchases.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotions drive quick sales, trial, and inventory clearance.

terms.definition: The retail convention of doubling delivered cost, so a $22 cost gets a $44 ticket. That one move is simultaneously a 100% markup on cost and exactly a 50% markup on retail, which is why the same practice gets quoted as two different percentages depending on the denominator.
terms.whyItMatters: Apparel and specialty-store pricing cases open with keystone as the starting ticket, then ask what margin survives after the item is marked down twice.

terms.definition: A tax structure whose rate rises as income rises, taxing each band of income at its own rate — the opposite of a regressive tax that takes a larger share from lower earners.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax-structure questions ask competitors to classify income tax, sales tax and payroll tax, and sales tax is regressive despite its single rate.

terms.definition: The ceiling on category demand in a defined area and period — every possible buyer times the maximum quantity each could buy times unit price; one firm's share of that ceiling is sales potential, and the volume it actually expects to sell on the funded budget is the sales forecast.
terms.whyItMatters: Sizing items on the marketing exam hand you a population, a purchase rate and a price and expect the whole-industry ceiling, not one company's number; in a market-identification roleplay the judge is listening for the three-step narrowing said in order.

terms.definition: The percentage of one brand's national sales made in a market divided by that market's percentage of national population, times 100; read against the category index it sorts markets into four actions — high BDI with low CDI means a strong brand in a weak category, while low BDI with high CDI is the classic opportunity market where the category sells well and the brand does not, and both indexes below 100 argues for withdrawal.
terms.whyItMatters: The paired index read is the standard answer to a roleplay asking which market to defend and which to invest in; giving one index without the other gets a follow-up you cannot answer.

terms.definition: Number of open opportunities multiplied by average deal size multiplied by win rate, all divided by the average sales cycle length in days, which yields revenue per day: 50 x $4,000 x 0.30 / 60 days = $1,000 a day. It is the one common metric where shortening the cycle raises revenue without adding a single new prospect.
terms.whyItMatters: When an exam item asks which of four fixes lifts revenue fastest, the velocity formula shows that cutting cycle time is a divisor change and beats a small win-rate gain.

terms.definition: Help-center or bot sessions that end without a human contact, divided by total sessions — 7,000 of 10,000 is 70%. A session only counts as deflected when no contact follows inside a set window, usually 24 hours; without that window an abandoned bot session where the customer gave up and phoned later is scored as a save.
terms.whyItMatters: The savings claim in a technology-in-CRM roleplay collapses without the follow-up window, and judges look for the competitor who states it.

terms.definition: Sum of the market shares of the four biggest sellers: 18 + 15 + 9 + 6 = 48%. Crossing roughly 40% marks an industry as an oligopoly, and 100% is a monopoly or a tight cartel — but because it adds shares without squaring them, it cannot tell four equal firms apart from one giant and three minnows.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition questions give a share table and ask for the structure label plus its threshold, and the blind spot is exactly what the follow-up tests.

terms.definition: A supplier-provided document in a fixed sixteen-section order under the Globally Harmonized System, covering hazards, handling, exposure controls, first aid and disposal — the fixed section order is the point, because a responder finds first-aid information in the same place on every sheet.
terms.whyItMatters: A chemical-spill roleplay expects you to say where the handling and first-aid instructions live and that the sheets must be accessible to employees on the shift, not filed in a manager's office.

terms.definition: A relationship in which one party acts on behalf of another party.
terms.whyItMatters: Businesses act through agents; competitors must grasp authority, liability, and duties.

terms.definition: Adds a new size, flavor, color, or form under an existing brand inside the category it already competes in; a brand extension instead carries that brand into a different category -- a cherry version of a cola is the first, a cola-branded snack chip is the second.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask you to grow a brand without new advertising weight; naming the wrong one of the pair gives away that you cannot tell same-category growth from category entry.

terms.definition: Minimum number of members who must be present for a body's votes to count — a majority of the membership under Robert's Rules unless the bylaws set something lower, often one third. Business conducted without one is void rather than merely defeated, so a motion that loses 3 to 2 stands as rejected while the same motion passed short of this number stands as nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A chapter-officer or board roleplay in which half the members skip the meeting is scored on whether the competitor recognizes that no decision can be made.

terms.definition: The percentage of sets actually in use that are tuned to a given program, so a show rating 6 in a market where only half the sets are on carries a 12 — the figure is always larger than the program's own rating because its denominator is smaller.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a rating and this figure for the same program and ask which one a national advertiser should buy against; the answer is the rating, because only it is measured against the full market a campaign is paying to cover.

terms.definition: Setting price by adding a standard markup to a product's cost.
terms.whyItMatters: It is a foundational method when a price must ensure cost recovery.

terms.definition: Total liabilities divided by owner's equity, showing how much of the business is financed by lenders rather than owners and how exposed it is to a downturn.
terms.whyItMatters: Financing scenarios ask whether a firm can take on another loan, and a high ratio is the reason a lender says no.

terms.definition: Letter layout that keeps the inside address, salutation, body paragraphs and any lists flush at the left margin but starts the dateline, complimentary close and signature block at the horizontal center of the page - about the 3-inch tab on a page with 1-inch margins. That one shifted column is the only difference from full block; adding a half-inch first-line indent to every paragraph converts it again into semi-block.
terms.whyItMatters: Formatting questions show the same letter three ways and score the competitor who can point to which elements moved, rather than judging the page by how balanced it looks.

terms.definition: Distinct customers who bought at least once in a period divided by the total defined target population, as a percentage — 40,000 buyers out of a 500,000-person target is 8% — which counts buyers, not units or dollars; that is exactly what separates it from market share, so a brand can raise share by selling more to the same people while its penetration does not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Growth roleplays hinge on whether the plan should recruit new buyers or sell more to current ones, and this is the number that tells the judge you know which lever you chose.

terms.definition: Asking questions to understand a customer's problems, goals, and requirements.
terms.whyItMatters: Assessing needs ensures recommendations truly solve the customer's problem.

terms.definition: A grid that derives a case's priority from how many people or how much revenue is affected, set against how fast the situation degrades — high impact with high urgency becomes P1, high impact with low urgency P2, and so on across a 3x3 or 4x4 grid. Priority is computed from the two axes rather than argued by whoever complains loudest.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a backlog of angry customers in a roleplay, the competitor who sorts by this grid instead of by volume of complaint wins the judged point on fairness.

terms.definition: (Price − marginal cost) ÷ price, running from 0 under perfect competition to near 1 for an unchallenged monopolist. A $50 price on $40 of marginal cost scores 0.20, and because the figure equals the reciprocal of demand elasticity, a firm facing elasticity of 5 can hold only a 20% markup over marginal cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing-power items ask how much a firm can charge above its own marginal cost, and the elasticity link converts a demand estimate into a markup ceiling.

terms.definition: An arrangement where the supplier monitors the buyer's usage data and decides replenishment timing and quantity, while the buyer still owns and pays for the stock on hand — consignment differs precisely there: the supplier retains ownership until the item is sold or consumed.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain collaboration roleplays ask who should hold the replenishment decision and who carries the cash tied up in the stock; the ownership line is what separates the two arrangements.

terms.term: French and Raven's five bases of power
terms.definition: Distinguishes five sources of influence — legitimate power from the position, reward power, coercive power, expert power from demonstrated knowledge, and referent power from personal respect — with the first three attached to the role and the last two to the individual. Expert and referent power produce commitment; coercive power produces compliance only while someone is watching.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking a new team lead with no formal authority to get cooperation is scored on building expert and referent power, and exam items on using power appropriately turn on that split.

terms.definition: Adds items between price or feature points a line already covers, usually to close a gap a rival occupies -- dropping a $600 model between the existing $450 and $850 units; line stretching instead pushes the line past the top or bottom of its current range.
terms.whyItMatters: A merchandising roleplay that reports a competitor winning a mid-price slot is scored on filling the gap rather than repricing the whole line.

terms.definition: Senior advocate who spends political capital on someone's behalf in rooms that person is not in, putting their name into promotion and staffing decisions and absorbing reputational risk if it goes badly. A mentor spends time instead of capital — advice given directly to you, with nothing of the mentor's own staked on the outcome.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on advancement patterns is scored on this distinction, because the competitor who only asks for coffee chats never gets named in the promotion meeting.

terms.definition: Direct, person-to-person communication to inform, persuade, and build relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: It enables customized pitches and problem-solving for high-value sales.

terms.definition: The percentage placed on goods when they first reach the floor, sized to absorb everything that will erode it: (operating expenses + profit + markdowns + employee discounts + shortages) / (net sales + markdowns + discounts + shortages). It is set deliberately higher than maintained markup because none of those reductions have happened yet.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-plan questions ask why a store tickets at 52% when it only expects to keep 40%, and the gap between this figure and maintained markup is the entire answer.

terms.definition: The payroll deduction funding Social Security and Medicare, taken at a fixed percentage of wages and matched dollar for dollar by the employer.
terms.whyItMatters: Pay-stub interpretation items ask why gross pay minus income tax still does not equal take-home pay, and FICA is the missing line.

terms.definition: Worker-days lost to unscheduled absence divided by (average number of employees times scheduled workdays), times 100 — 96 days lost across 40 employees over 20 workdays is 96/800, or 12%. Scheduled vacation and approved leave stay out of the numerator, which is why a business with generous paid time off can still post a low rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations roleplays ask you to quantify an attendance problem before proposing a policy; the ratio is what turns supervisor complaints into a defensible number.

terms.definition: The core marketing activities such as pricing, promotion, selling, and distribution.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors organize their analysis around which marketing functions a decision touches.

terms.definition: Units of a specific add-on sold divided by units of the primary product sold, times 100 — 300 protection plans on 1,000 phones is 30%. It scores one named pairing, where cross-sell measurement counts every additional category a customer buys, so a store can raise total cross-sell revenue while this figure falls.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays that set an accessories goal are graded on whether you name the ratio you will move and the counter behavior that moves it, not on a general promise to sell more.

terms.definition: A total outage or safety-affecting failure with no workaround, carrying the tightest published clock — commonly a 15-minute acknowledgement, hourly status updates and continuous work until restoration. Severity rates the technical damage while priority adds business context, so a Sev-1 affecting one tiny account can still be worked at P2.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-level roleplays hinge on the severity-versus-priority split, and quoting the acknowledgement clock is what makes the answer specific rather than reassuring.

terms.definition: Extra output produced by one more worker, computed as the change in quantity divided by the change in workers. Going from 4 to 5 employees and from 40 to 46 units gives 6. It also sets marginal cost: at a $120 daily wage, that worker's units cost 120 ÷ 6 = $20 each, so cost per unit rises the moment the added output starts shrinking.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing and productivity items ask what one more scheduled worker actually adds and what that output costs, which is where diminishing returns become dollars.

terms.definition: Recordable injuries and illnesses multiplied by 200,000, divided by total hours worked — the 200,000 representing 100 full-time employees working a 2,000-hour year, which is what makes a small firm's figure comparable with a large one's.
terms.whyItMatters: Safety roleplays give an injury count and an hours-worked total and ask whether the site is above its industry benchmark; a raw injury count cannot be benchmarked and is scored as an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: A warehouse layout placing one central fact table of numeric measures among denormalized dimension tables, each exactly one join away from the facts; the snowflake variant normalizes those dimensions into further sub-tables, which saves storage and removes redundancy but adds a join to every query that touches them.
terms.whyItMatters: A database-design item shows a sales fact table ringed by product, store and date tables and asks why the dimensions repeat values instead of being split further.

terms.definition: How a product is differentiated in the market and in customers' minds.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear positioning conveys unique value and targets the right segments.

terms.definition: Prompt demanding a specific past incident, on the premise that past behavior predicts future behavior, with answers scored against written anchors — which is why a hypothetical answer earns zero. A situational question does the opposite, asking what you would do in a scenario you have never faced, and is scored for reasoning rather than evidence.
terms.whyItMatters: The interview portion of a job-seeking roleplay is graded on giving a dated, quantified incident when the question asks for one, not a description of your general habits.

terms.definition: The number of exposures needed inside a single purchase cycle before a message registers at all — below it the spend is wasted and above it the spend is redundant. The working planning standard is three exposures, from Krugman's three-hit theory.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a client wants the budget spread over more vehicles is a test of this: adding vehicles raises reach but can drop everyone below three exposures, leaving a campaign that technically touched the market and communicated nothing.

terms.definition: Setting a high initial price to earn maximum revenue from eager buyers.
terms.whyItMatters: Skimming fits new or innovative products willing buyers will pay for.

terms.definition: Net income divided by owner's equity, measuring profit generated per dollar the owners have invested rather than per dollar of sales.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items compare two firms with equal profits and different equity bases; the one earning more per invested dollar wins.

terms.definition: Separating a business unit into an independent company by distributing its shares to existing shareholders, who receive no cash and simply hold two stocks instead of one; a divestiture sells the unit to an outside buyer and brings cash into the parent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask which restructuring raises capital for the parent, and the tested distinction is that only the sale does while the share distribution does not.

terms.definition: The top rung of the three-stage loyalty ladder: at recognition the buyer merely knows the mark, at preference the buyer chooses it but accepts a substitute when it is out of stock, and at insistence the buyer will leave the store or delay the purchase rather than take another brand — the only stage that lets a firm hold price through a competitor's promotion.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask what a strong brand is actually worth; naming the three stages and the out-of-stock behavior that separates preference from insistence is what earns the point.

terms.definition: A product's characteristics and the value those characteristics give.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must separate features from benefits to sell effectively.

terms.definition: The contractual penalty owed when a provider misses its service-level target — typically 10% of the monthly fee for the first missed tier, rising by band and capped at 100%. In most agreements it is the customer's sole remedy, and it must be claimed inside a stated window, often 30 days, or the right to it lapses entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business account roleplay, the competitor who knows the credit must be requested rather than issued automatically recovers real money for the client.

terms.definition: Keep producing while the revenue the next unit brings in exceeds the cost it adds, and stop at the output where the two are equal. If the next unit adds $12 of revenue and $9 of cost, making it gains $3; past the crossing point each extra unit subtracts from profit even though total revenue is still rising.
terms.whyItMatters: Factors-affecting-profit items ask for the quantity a firm should produce from a marginal cost and marginal revenue schedule, not from total revenue.

terms.definition: A formal document requesting goods or services from a vendor at set terms.
terms.whyItMatters: Purchase orders create the paper trail for efficient procurement.

terms.definition: Discovering and defining the markets where a business can sell its offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Identifying the right market is the foundation of any marketing plan.

terms.definition: Extends a line beyond the price range it now serves -- downward into cheaper segments, upward into premium ones, or both at once, as when a marque starting at $30,000 adds a $19,000 entry car; line filling by contrast stays entirely inside the range already covered.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays warn about trading down: stretching downward risks the parent brand's image, and judges look for that risk named alongside the volume it buys.

terms.definition: Cover document sent with an application to a posted opening, naming the requisition and tying two or three of its stated requirements to specific evidence from your record. A letter of inquiry does the same job for a company with no advertised opening, so it opens with the employer's problem instead of with a listing.
terms.whyItMatters: A written-event or job-search roleplay that supplies a job posting expects the letter to answer that posting's requirements point by point.

terms.definition: Activities that build positive relationships with the public and media.
terms.whyItMatters: PR manages image, trust, and credibility through third-party voices.

terms.definition: What the retailer actually keeps once reductions are taken: net sales minus gross cost of goods sold, stated as a percent of net sales. It sits below initial markup by the amount of markdowns, shortages and employee discounts, and it - not the original ticket - is the margin that has to cover operating expenses.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance and marketing exams give the initial markup plus a markdown total and ask for the margin that survived, which is this number rather than the one on the price tag.

terms.definition: Net income available to common shareholders divided by shares outstanding, the per-share figure that lets companies of different sizes be compared.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment scenarios quote it as the headline number, and a competitor is expected to know a buyback raises it without any change in profit.

terms.definition: Attaches automatically under UCC section 2-314 whenever the seller is a merchant dealing in goods of that kind, promising the goods are fit for their ordinary purpose, adequately packaged and labeled, and of fair average quality. Its near neighbour, the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose under section 2-315, arises only when the seller knows the buyer's special use and the buyer relies on the seller to select — and that one binds non-merchant sellers too.
terms.whyItMatters: Product-complaint roleplays ask which warranty a customer can still invoke when the receipt says nothing about quality at all.

terms.definition: The added value a strong, well-known brand name gives a product.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand equity explains why customers pay more for, and stay loyal to, established brands.

terms.definition: A six-part qualification framework — Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Champion — that adds the buyer's internal mechanics, the written criteria and the approval path, to the money-and-authority checks BANT stops at. It is built for long committee purchases where the signer is never the first contact.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business roleplay with a committee, naming the economic buyer and the decision criteria is the specific step judges look for before any presentation content.

terms.definition: The finding that a customer whose problem is fixed exceptionally well can finish more loyal than one who never had a problem — but it holds only for a first, low-severity failure resolved fast by someone empowered to fix it on the spot. On a repeat failure the effect reverses and satisfaction lands below the never-failed baseline, so engineering failures is never the strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint roleplays reward naming the condition; a competitor who claims the paradox always applies is marked down for it.

terms.definition: Keep the doors open in the short run only while price covers average variable cost; at a lower price closing loses less, because fixed costs are owed either way. At $8 price with $7 variable and $4 fixed cost per unit, the firm loses $3 a unit but still operates, since shutting down would lose the full $4.
terms.whyItMatters: Operating-cost roleplays ask whether a location losing money should close now; the test is variable cost coverage, not whether the site is profitable.

terms.definition: How many times inventory is sold and replaced over a period.
terms.whyItMatters: Turnover reveals inventory efficiency and its impact on cash flow.

terms.definition: Trompenaars' pole opposite universalism: which rule applies depends on the relationship and the circumstance, so a signed contract is a starting point a long-standing partner may reopen, and an obligation to a friend can outrank written policy. Universalist cultures - the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Germany - hold that one standard binds everyone regardless of who is asking, which is why the identical request reads as reasonable flexibility on one side of the table and as favoritism on the other.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay where a long-time distributor asks for terms no other account receives is scored on naming the cultural logic at work before ruling on the request.

terms.definition: Creating a distinct name, symbol, and image for a specific offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Product branding helps customers identify and prefer that offering.

terms.definition: The information return a business files for every non-employee it paid $600 or more for services in a calendar year, furnished to both the worker and the IRS by January 31. Nothing is withheld, so the contractor carries the whole 15.3% self-employment tax (12.4% Social Security + 2.9% Medicare) and pays it in quarterly estimates, whereas a Form W-2 employee splits that load with an employer paying 7.65%; a payee who supplies no taxpayer ID triggers 24% backup withholding.
terms.whyItMatters: Career-cluster exam items ask what changes when a firm hires a freelance designer instead of a staff one, and a professional-development roleplay where the judge plays a first-time gig worker is graded on naming the $600 filing trigger and the fact that no tax comes out of the check.

terms.definition: The share of the target exposed at or above the threshold number of times — conventionally three or more — so a schedule with 70% total reach may deliver only 35% of this, because the half of the audience that saw the ad once or twice does not count toward it.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-plan items give a reach curve and a frequency distribution and ask which of two schedules performs better; the one with lower total reach usually wins because more of its audience cleared the three-exposure threshold.

terms.definition: Reduction dollars measured against actual net sales rather than against the original ticket: dollar markdown / net sales. The off-retail version instead divides the reduction by the original price, so a $20 cut on a $50 item is a 40% off-retail markdown but a different number in the store's markdown-to-sales figure.
terms.whyItMatters: Clearance-planning roleplays require a candidate to say which denominator they used before a judge will accept the percentage they quote.

terms.definition: A retirement account whose contributions escape tax now and whose withdrawals are taxed later, trading a deduction today for taxable income in retirement.
terms.whyItMatters: Retirement-planning roleplays turn on when the client wants the tax bill, which is the whole traditional-versus-Roth decision.

terms.definition: Leading by modeling integrity, fairness, and moral principles.
terms.whyItMatters: It builds organizational trust and sets the tone for employee behavior.

terms.definition: Attributes a brand must match well enough for buyers to accept it as a legitimate member of the category — a car that is safe, a bank that clears deposits — which buy entry and win no preference at all; the attributes that win preference are points of difference, and because parity is a threshold rather than a scale, money spent beating a rival on a parity attribute returns nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking where to invest a product-improvement budget is a parity-versus-difference question; spending to over-deliver on a category minimum is the error the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: A method built on teach, tailor and take control, in which the rep opens with a commercial insight that reframes how the buyer sees their own business and then respectfully pushes back on the buyer's assumptions. Relationship selling does the reverse: it builds trust first and delivers whatever the buyer already says they want.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay judged on demonstrating expertise rewards teaching the buyer something about their own market, while a purely agreeable rep reads as an order taker.

terms.definition: The measured gap between complaints received and customers actually dissatisfied — the classic TARP studies put the share of unhappy customers who bother to complain at roughly 4 in 100, so one voiced complaint stands in for about two dozen silent defectors. A falling complaint count can therefore signal abandonment rather than improvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay that celebrates fewer complaints needs this correction, and it is the argument that funds proactive outreach.

terms.definition: Selling price multiplied by the extra output the next worker adds — $15 a unit times 6 units is $90 a day. Hire while that figure is at or above the wage and stop when it drops below: at a $100 wage this worker is not worth adding, even though the worker before, adding 9 units and $135, clearly was.
terms.whyItMatters: Labor and productivity questions ask how many people a firm should employ, and the comparison of this figure to the wage is the tested rule.

terms.definition: Inspecting products and services to ensure they meet set standards.
terms.whyItMatters: It catches defects early, protecting satisfaction and reducing waste.

terms.definition: Programs that build employee skills and knowledge for current and future roles.
terms.whyItMatters: Training improves performance, cuts turnover, and prepares people for advancement.

terms.definition: Cuts slow items from a line by ranked contribution rather than by unit volume, acting on the common finding that the bottom half of a catalog produces under 5% of sales; the deciding test is what share of a cut item's buyers switch to a surviving item instead of to a rival.
terms.whyItMatters: An assortment roleplay hands you a sales-by-item list; the winning answer cuts on contribution and states the transfer assumption, because a high-volume item can carry almost no margin.

terms.definition: Software that parses every application into structured fields and ranks candidates by keyword match against the requisition before a recruiter reads a single one. Multi-column layouts, text inside images and invented section headings are dropped during parsing, so a qualified candidate can be screened out by formatting rather than by qualifications.
terms.whyItMatters: A job-search roleplay advising a competitor whose applications get no response usually turns on this filter, not on the strength of the experience.

terms.definition: Unpaid media coverage generated through PR, news, and referrals.
terms.whyItMatters: Publicity builds credibility through sources other than paid ads.

terms.definition: Setting a low initial price to gain market share and deter competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: Penetration helps when entering a new market or fighting competition.

terms.definition: Share price divided by earnings per share, the number of dollars investors pay for each dollar of annual profit — a rough gauge of how much growth is priced in.
terms.whyItMatters: Advising a client on whether a stock looks expensive in an investing roleplay turns on this multiple, not on the share price alone.

terms.definition: Documents and files that capture a business's transactions, operations, and decisions.
terms.whyItMatters: Accurate records are required for compliance, accountability, and historical reference.

terms.definition: Attributes buyers strongly associate with one brand, rate favorably, and believe no competitor delivers as well — all three conditions, not just the first — which is what makes them the reason to choose it, unlike points of parity, which only qualify the brand for the consideration set; once rivals match a claimed difference it has quietly become a parity attribute and stops moving share even though the advertising still runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to identify what sets a company apart, a competitor who names a feature every rival also offers has named a parity attribute and will be corrected on the spot.

terms.definition: Connecting a product feature to the benefit the customer receives.
terms.whyItMatters: It turns product facts into customer value.

terms.definition: Lapsed customers who return after a targeted campaign, divided by lapsed customers contacted — 120 of 2,000 is 6%. It usually beats new acquisition on cost because the contact data and purchase history are already owned, but only when the offer answers the stated reason for leaving rather than simply discounting the same product.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay asks which list gets the budget, and this rate weighed against customer acquisition cost is the comparison judges expect.

terms.definition: The smallest output at which long-run average cost stops falling and flattens out. If unit cost drops from $9 to $6 between 10,000 and 50,000 units and then holds at $6, the threshold is 50,000 — a rival producing 20,000 pays $7 or $8 and cannot match a $6.50 price, which is how the number becomes an entry barrier.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition items ask why a small entrant cannot match an incumbent's price, and the expected answer is the output threshold, not brand loyalty.

terms.definition: The square root of (2 x annual demand x cost per order) divided by annual holding cost per unit — the single order size where rising carrying cost and falling ordering cost cross and total cost bottoms out.
terms.whyItMatters: An operations roleplay that asks you to cut the cost of holding stock is answered with this trade-off, not with 'order less': you must say that ordering more often lowers carrying cost but raises order cost, and name the quantity where the two balance.

terms.definition: A semi-autonomous division with its own mission, competitors, and profit responsibility, planned as if it were a standalone business inside the parent; it is the unit of analysis a portfolio matrix plots, which a functional department such as accounting can never be.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask what is placed in the cells of a portfolio grid, and the tested error is plotting departments or individual products instead.

terms.definition: Methods such as brainstorming and focus groups used to create product concepts.
terms.whyItMatters: Structured idea generation yields higher-quality innovations.
