terms.definition: A route into a second state's professional licence that accepts a licence already held in good standing elsewhere — for CPAs, commonly practice in four of the last ten years plus education and exam requirements the receiving board judges substantially equivalent — instead of requiring the applicant to sit that state's own examination again. It runs one direction only, which is what separates it from reciprocity: the receiving state grants the privilege and the sending state owes nothing in return.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance roleplay in which the judge plays an accountant relocating for a promotion turns on whether they must re-test, and exam items on advancement patterns expect this route named rather than a vague 'get licensed again.'

terms.definition: A schedule carrying a low continuous weight all year with heavier bursts layered over the peak selling weeks, so unlike flighting the brand is never entirely off air, and unlike continuity the weekly weight is not flat.
terms.whyItMatters: A client with year-round sales and a holiday spike is the standard prompt for this pattern; naming it and drawing the line against the other two schedules is what separates a scored answer from a vague one.

terms.term: Gross margin return on inventory investment (GMROI)
terms.definition: Ties margin to the money tied up in stock: gross margin dollars / average inventory at cost, which equals gross-margin percent multiplied by the sales-to-stock ratio. A result of 3.00 means three dollars of margin per dollar invested, whereas inventory turnover counts how often stock sells and says nothing about the margin earned each turn.
terms.whyItMatters: A buyer's roleplay compares two vendors with identical turnover and different margins, and this is the single figure that separates them for the judge.

terms.definition: A retirement account funded with money already taxed, whose qualified withdrawals — contributions and growth alike — come out tax-free.
terms.whyItMatters: Advising a young client in a retirement roleplay usually points here, because decades of growth escape tax when the current bracket is low.

terms.definition: One company's maximum obtainable slice of category demand — market potential multiplied by the highest share it could hold with unlimited marketing effort; it always sits above the sales forecast, which discounts that ceiling down to the effort and budget actually approved.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that give an industry ceiling and a best-case share expect this middle figure, and a competitor who reports it as the forecast overstates the plan's revenue line in front of a judge.

terms.definition: The percentage of total sales in a market captured by one business or product.
terms.whyItMatters: Market share quantifies competitive position and the payoff of a growth strategy.

terms.definition: An advance paid to a rep against commission not yet earned — a $3,000 monthly draw against $2,200 of earnings leaves $800 outstanding. A recoverable draw carries that $800 forward against next month's commissions, while a non-recoverable draw forgives it, which makes the second version a guaranteed minimum in everything but name.
terms.whyItMatters: Human-resources and selling exam items ask which pay plan protects a new rep during a long ramp, and the recoverable-versus-non-recoverable distinction is the answer's hinge.

terms.definition: A refund, credit or replacement granted where the company owes nothing contractually — outside warranty, past the return window, or where the customer caused the damage. It is expensed as a service or marketing cost rather than charged against the warranty reserve, which is why finance tracks it separately and caps each agent's authority in dollars.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the customer's claim is genuinely out of policy tests whether the competitor can grant an exception and state what it costs the company.

terms.definition: Gap between what buyers would have paid and what they did pay, measured as the area under the demand curve and above the market price. With demand starting at $50, a $20 price and 300 units sold, it equals ½ × 300 × ($50 − $20) = $4,500 — and a price rise to $30 cuts it, which is the value a seller captures when it segments buyers.
terms.whyItMatters: Price-function questions ask what buyers lose when a price rises or a shortage appears; the triangle turns that into a dollar figure.

terms.definition: Planning, executing, and monitoring work to hit objectives within time and budget.
terms.whyItMatters: It lets managers coordinate resources and deliver on schedule.

terms.definition: Federal law policing written warranties on consumer products: one costing more than $10 must be designated conspicuously as full or limited, terms must be available to read before purchase on products over $15, a full warranty may not shorten the duration of implied warranties, and issuing any written warranty strips the seller of the power to disclaim implied warranties. It also lets a prevailing consumer recover attorney fees, which is why small warranty claims get litigated at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays about extended service plans test whether a store that printed a warranty can still sell the item as is — under this Act it cannot.

terms.definition: Cuts promotion, development, and service spending on a declining item toward zero while continuing to sell it, milking cash from the buyers who remain; divestment instead sells or discontinues the item outright, freeing shelf space and capital at once but ending that cash stream immediately.
terms.whyItMatters: Life-cycle roleplays put a fading item in front of you and score whether you choose between milking it and killing it, with a reason tied to remaining loyal demand.

terms.definition: Degree program alternating full-time paid work terms with academic terms, where the work terms carry academic credit and a faculty evaluation. An internship is a single standalone placement with no required academic component, which is why students on this track often graduate with a year or more of documented, evaluated experience.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on ways to build work experience while still in school is scored on distinguishing the credit-bearing alternating program from a one-off summer job.

terms.definition: The channels ads run on — TV, radio, print, digital, outdoor, and social.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the right media reaches the target audience cost-effectively.

terms.definition: Using prices like $9.99 to shape customer perception of value.
terms.whyItMatters: It shows how price presentation affects customer behavior and sales.

terms.definition: Annual dividends per share divided by share price, stating income return as a percentage so a dividend stock can be compared against a savings rate.
terms.whyItMatters: A client asking for income rather than growth in a retirement roleplay is asking about this figure, which moves whenever the share price moves.

terms.definition: The identity and reputation a person projects through their online presence.
terms.whyItMatters: A personal social media brand can boost or damage credibility.

terms.definition: A brand architecture in which the corporate name stays off the products and each brand carries its own separate equity — Procter & Gamble's Tide, Pampers and Gillette show no visible parent — which is the opposite of a branded house, where one master name fronts every offering; the trade-off is that a failure in one brand cannot contaminate the others, paid for by funding awareness separately for each name.
terms.whyItMatters: Corporate-branding roleplays ask whether a new line should carry the parent name; the answer turns on this architecture choice and the contamination risk it prices.

terms.definition: A structured pitch showing how an offering meets the customer's needs.
terms.whyItMatters: A compelling presentation moves a prospect toward purchase.

terms.definition: The share of customers who buy again inside a defined window, counted per purchase occasion — 30 of 100 first-time buyers ordering again within 90 days is 30%. Retention rate counts customers still active at period end whether or not they bought anything, so a subscription can post 95% retention alongside a repurchase rate of zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty cases mix the two constantly, and naming the difference in the denominator is the discriminating answer a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Area between the equal-shares diagonal and the actual income curve, divided by the whole triangle under that diagonal, giving 0 for identical incomes and 1 for one household holding everything. A move from 0.38 to 0.45 means income concentrated, and since it is a ratio it says nothing about whether anyone got richer.
terms.whyItMatters: Economic-development items compare two markets' income spread to pick a target segment, and the score is the measure they hand you.

terms.definition: Average daily usage multiplied by lead time in days, plus safety stock — the on-hand level that triggers a replenishment order, so it answers WHEN to order while economic order quantity answers HOW MUCH.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give you daily usage, a supplier lead time and a buffer and ask at what stock level a buyer should place the reorder; picking the order size instead of the trigger level is the standard wrong answer.

terms.definition: Models trustworthiness as credibility plus reliability plus intimacy, all divided by self-orientation — so visibly acting in your own interest divides away everything the other three terms earn. Credibility is about words, reliability about repeated actions over time, and intimacy about safety in disclosure, which is why a person can be believable and still not be trusted.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on rebuilding a client or coworker relationship is scored on lowering the self-orientation term — leading with their problem — rather than on producing more credentials.

terms.definition: Lifts a mature item's sales by changing who buys it or how often rather than changing the item: volume equals users times usage rate, so new user segments, new uses, and more use per occasion are the three levers; product modification instead alters the item's quality, features, or style.
terms.whyItMatters: Maturity-stage questions ask what a marketer does when sales flatten; the pair of levers must be told apart, since a judge hears 'add a feature' as the other strategy entirely.

terms.definition: Planning credential CFP Board grants to a candidate who holds a bachelor's degree, completes registered coursework, passes a 170-question exam given in two three-hour sessions, and logs 6,000 hours of professional experience — or 4,000 hours under a supervised apprenticeship — then renews with 30 continuing-education hours every two years, 2 of them CFP Board ethics. Against a licence that only obliges a recommendation to be suitable, the difference is the standard of care: the holder must act as a fiduciary and place the client's interest ahead of their own whenever advice is given.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance roleplays that make a competitor explain designations to a client reward the fiduciary-versus-suitability line, and exam items on ongoing education use the 30-hour, two-year renewal as the tested number.

terms.definition: Media cost divided by impressions delivered and multiplied by 1,000 — a $6,000 magazine page reaching 400,000 readers is $15 — the conversion that makes a cheap small vehicle and an expensive large one directly comparable.
terms.whyItMatters: The most common media-math item on the marketing exam gives two vehicles with different prices and different audiences and asks which is the better buy; the raw price answers nothing and this figure answers it in one step.

terms.definition: Selling price minus variable cost per unit - the dollars each extra sale releases to cover fixed costs and then profit. Gross profit per unit subtracts the full cost of goods sold instead, charging the unit for fixed manufacturing cost that this measure deliberately leaves out.
terms.whyItMatters: Every break-even item on the finance exam needs this figure first, and a competitor who reaches for gross profit computes a break-even volume that is too high.

terms.definition: The sum of a project's future cash flows discounted back to today's dollars, minus its initial cost — positive means the project earns more than the required return.
terms.whyItMatters: Capital-investment items ask whether to buy the equipment, and the sign of this figure is the answer regardless of how large the raw cash flows look.

terms.definition: (Monetary benefit of the program minus program cost) divided by program cost, times 100 — a $60,000 gain from a $20,000 course is (60,000 - 20,000)/20,000, or 200%. The benefit must be converted to dollars first, typically from reduced error rates or faster ramp time, which is the step that separates it from a satisfaction score collected at the end of class.
terms.whyItMatters: A training-proposal roleplay is scored on converting the learning gain into dollars and dividing by cost, not on describing how much participants enjoyed the session.

terms.definition: Divides a market by activities, interests, opinions, values and lifestyle captured through AIO inventories, unlike demographic segmentation, which uses census-verifiable facts such as age, income and household size; two 34-year-olds each earning $60,000 fall in one demographic cell and can still land in opposite psychographic segments, which is why demographics alone cannot explain why one buys the premium line.
terms.whyItMatters: A market-planning roleplay that hands you a customer base and asks for a segmentation base is scored on naming the base and defending it against the other three; the usual failure is calling lifestyle data 'demographics'.

terms.definition: A higher commission rate applied only to revenue above quota — 8% up to plan and 12% beyond it — so each dollar of overperformance pays more than the first dollar did. A cap or a decelerator does the reverse and is precisely what tempts a rep to hold a signed deal until the next period opens.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on motivating a sales force ask which plan change stops sandbagging at quarter end, and the rate structure above quota is the mechanism being tested.

terms.definition: A published schedule matching the size of the failure to the size of the fix — apology plus correction for a minor first delay, a partial credit of roughly 10% to 25% of the transaction for a repeat, and a full refund plus a retention offer where the failure cost the customer money. It keeps compensation consistent and stops the loudest complainer being paid the most.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges in complaint roleplays reward a proportionate remedy; naming the rung and its value beats offering a blanket refund every time.

terms.definition: Allocate a budget so the last dollar spent on each good returns the same added satisfaction: MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py. If one item returns 20 utils per dollar and another 10, shifting spending toward the first raises total satisfaction until the two ratios meet — the rule that produces the downward-sloping demand curve.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-behavior roleplays ask why a shopper walked away from the better product; the per-dollar comparison, not the raw benefit, explains the switch.

terms.definition: Measures that protect confidential business and customer information from unauthorized access.
terms.whyItMatters: Good data security prevents costly breaches and keeps trust.

terms.definition: A descriptive attribute that changes over time and forces a documented choice: Type 1 overwrites the old value and loses all history, while Type 2 closes the existing row with an end date and inserts a new version row, so a sale made two years ago still ties to the sales territory that was in force on the day it happened.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay judge asks why last year's totals shifted after a store was reassigned to a new district, the answer is which of these two handling types the warehouse used.

terms.definition: Promises to repair, replace, or refund a product that fails to meet terms.
terms.whyItMatters: They reduce customer risk and signal confidence in quality.

terms.definition: The cap a registered apprenticeship program's standards must state under 29 CFR Part 29 on how many apprentices may work per experienced worker on a job — one to one is the common floor, and a sponsor that exceeds its registered figure risks deregistration of the whole program. It travels with a stepped wage schedule: the apprentice begins near 50% of the journeyworker rate and moves up at fixed hour milestones, so the sponsor's cost per apprentice climbs across the term rather than staying flat.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how a small contractor can afford to train new workers is answered with the supervision ratio and the stepped percentage, and exam items pair it with registered apprenticeship to test whether the competitor knows the arrangement is federally regulated rather than an informal handshake.

terms.definition: What one rating point of a market costs: spot price divided by the program's rating, so a $3,000 spot on a 5-rated program is $600. It prices a percentage of a market where cost per thousand prices raw impressions, which is why it cannot be compared across markets of different sizes.
terms.whyItMatters: Broadcast-buying items ask a competitor to rank stations within one market, where this is the right measure, then ask to compare a small market against a large one, where it is the wrong one and cost per thousand is needed instead.

terms.definition: Stated as a share of the selling price rather than in dollars: (price - variable cost) / price, or total contribution / total sales. It converts a dollar sales target straight into profit, and it differs from a gross margin ratio because only genuinely variable costs are subtracted from revenue.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks how much additional revenue is needed to fund a $5,000 promotion is solved by dividing that spend by this ratio, not by the gross margin.

terms.definition: Investing a fixed amount on a fixed schedule regardless of price, which buys more shares when prices are low and lowers the average cost per share over time.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment roleplays ask how a client should handle a volatile market, and this is the answer that beats trying to time an entry point.

terms.definition: A combination of firms in unrelated industries, pursued for earnings diversification rather than operating synergy; a horizontal merger joins direct competitors at the same stage, and a vertical merger joins a buyer with its own supplier or distributor.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items name the two merging firms' industries and ask for the merger type, because each type draws different antitrust scrutiny.

terms.definition: A brand architecture where one master name fronts every offering and the sub-offerings are descriptors rather than brands — Google Maps, Google Drive, FedEx Freight — so every dollar of marketing on any one product raises awareness for all of them; the opposing structure is a house of brands, where each product owns its equity and one scandal is quarantined to a single name instead of reaching the whole portfolio.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay weighing a launch's branding cost against its risk is decided by naming both architectures and the efficiency-versus-contagion trade between them.

terms.definition: Responding to a customer's concerns in a helpful, persuasive way.
terms.whyItMatters: Handling objections improves trust and conversion.

terms.definition: The support, delivery, returns and account-management cost attributable to one customer or segment, subtracted after cost of goods before any margin judgement — a segment buying $50,000 at 30% gross margin but generating $12,000 of returns and service calls earns $3,000, not $15,000. Revenue rank and profit rank routinely disagree because of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains why the largest account in a case can be the unprofitable one, and any roleplay recommending a service fee or a channel change for that account has to show this subtraction.

terms.definition: Tangible products in limited supply that must be produced and purchased.
terms.whyItMatters: Distinguishing goods from services underlies every business model.

terms.definition: Buffer units sized as a service-level z-value times the standard deviation of demand over lead time, held only to absorb variability — unlike cycle stock, which is the working quantity consumed between deliveries and would exist even with perfectly steady demand.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier-reliability roleplay turns on this: raising the promised in-stock service level raises the buffer more than proportionally, so the judge wants the cost of that extra protection weighed against the cost of a stockout.

terms.definition: Sizing demand from the bottom up: identify every potential buyer in each segment or territory, estimate units each would buy, and sum units times price across them. The chain-ratio method runs the opposite direction, starting from a national total and multiplying it down through successive percentages.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business sizing cases on the exam name a count of establishments and a per-establishment purchase rate, which is a buildup problem; using a national percentage chain there produces the wrong answer.

terms.definition: Puts a written or drawn description of an unbuilt product before target buyers and scores stated purchase intent, normally reading the top two boxes of a 5-point scale -- 'definitely' plus 'probably would buy' -- then discounting that figure, because stated intent runs far above actual trial.
terms.whyItMatters: Feasibility roleplays ask how you would test an idea before building it; naming the intent scale and the discount separates a real answer from 'ask some customers.'

terms.term: Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act
terms.definition: Federal statute obliging an employer of 100 or more employees to give 60 calendar days' written notice before a plant closing that ends 50 or more jobs at one site within any 30-day window, or a mass layoff of 500 workers — or of 50 to 499 when that reaches a third of the site's active workforce. Skipping notice is not a fine paid to the government: the remedy is back pay and benefits owed to each affected worker for every day of shortfall, capped at 60.
terms.whyItMatters: Worker-rights exam items use the 60-day count to kill distractors, and a professional-development roleplay where the judge plays an employee hearing closing rumors is scored on stating the notice entitlement and the back-pay remedy instead of offering reassurance.

terms.definition: Targeted messages sent straight to individuals by mail, email, or phone.
terms.whyItMatters: Direct marketing allows personalized, measurable, one-to-one engagement.

terms.definition: Setting prices based on what competitors charge for similar products.
terms.whyItMatters: It is essential for positioning and staying competitive.

terms.definition: The percentage used to convert a future dollar into today's dollars; raising it lowers the present value of every future cash flow and can flip a project from worth doing to not.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the input that makes a net-present-value question answerable, and exam items test that a riskier project carries a higher one.

terms.definition: A legal entity separate from its owners that can own property, contract, and be sued.
terms.whyItMatters: Incorporation shields owners from personal liability for business debts.

terms.definition: A product brand that leads with its own name while carrying a visible parent guarantee — Courtyard by Marriott, Polo by Ralph Lauren — sitting between a house of brands, where no parent is shown at all, and a sub-brand, where the parent name leads and the descriptor trails, as in Microsoft Office; the endorsement lends credibility without forcing the parent to own the product's positioning.
terms.whyItMatters: Hotel and hospitality roleplays about launching a new tier are answered with this middle structure, and judges expect the sub-brand contrast to be drawn explicitly.

terms.definition: Sizing territories by the work each contains: accounts multiplied by the calls per year each requires, divided by the calls one rep can make — 400 accounts needing 12 calls each is 4,800 calls, and at 800 calls per rep that is six territories. The breakdown method instead divides a sales forecast by average revenue per rep and ignores how much service each account demands.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay asking you to rebalance territories after a merger wants the calculation and the service load, not an even split of the map.

terms.definition: Customers who bring in at least one new paying customer, divided by total customers — 400 of 8,000 is 5%, and it can never exceed 100% because it counts referrers. The viral coefficient counts new customers produced per existing customer instead, so it can exceed 1; quoting one where the other belongs makes a growth forecast impossible.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth roleplays ask for a measurable target, and the wrong one of the two makes the projection arithmetically unachievable.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by the required reserve ratio, and caps how far one new deposit can expand the money supply: at a 10% reserve ratio the multiplier is 10, so $1,000 of fresh reserves can support up to $10,000 of deposits. Cash held outside banks and excess reserves both shrink the real-world figure below the formula.
terms.whyItMatters: Macro items that hand you a reserve ratio and a deposit want this reciprocal computed, and the deposit-expansion number is graded, not the explanation of lending.

terms.definition: The ongoing expenses of running a business — labor, materials, utilities, maintenance.
terms.whyItMatters: Controlling operating costs is a lever competitors use to lift profit.

terms.definition: A gesture carrying a fixed verbal translation that works with no speech at all - a thumbs-up, a head shake, the finger-and-thumb ring - which is precisely what separates it from an illustrator, a gesture that means nothing apart from the words it accompanies, such as sketching a package's size in the air. Because the translation is assigned by culture rather than by resemblance, this type can invert across a border: the same ring means money in Japan and is obscene in Brazil.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay that has you demonstrate a product to a foreign buyer is scored on choosing gestures whose meaning does not flip, and exam items ask which gesture type still communicates when used silently.

terms.definition: Laws and rules ensuring fair practices and safeguarding customer rights.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding it helps a business operate ethically and avoid liability.
